name: Milvus
description:
Milvus follows a foundation-managed Open-Core distribution model, similar to projects like Apache Spark or Kubernetes. This model is built around two distinct offerings:
The open-source core (100% free): Milvus is entirely free under the Apache 2.0 license. Any company can install and scale it on its own servers without paying licensing fees.
Zilliz Cloud (paid / SaaS): This is the fully managed commercial offering. Zilliz charges for infrastructure, automation, enterprise-grade security (such as RBAC and advanced encryption), and technical support to run Milvus on cloud platforms like AWS, GCP, and Azure.
In 2026, the commercial offering evolved into a "Vector Lakebase" model, enabling the indexing and analysis of massive datasets directly where they reside (in formats like Parquet or Iceberg) without requiring data duplication. Milvus positions itself as a major industrial player.
Milvus is the world’s most popular open-source vector database, with over 44,000 stars on GitHub. It is specifically designed for processing billions of vectors. Its distributed architecture sets it apart: unlike Qdrant, which is lightweight and monolithic, Milvus completely separates compute nodes, indexing nodes, and storage. This makes it highly scalable but also complex to manage in DevOps, requiring Kubernetes in production environments.
Finally, Milvus stands out for its native support for GPU hardware acceleration, enabling similarity computations and indexing at exceptional speeds.

name: AutoDesk
description:
Autodesk’s history is one of democratizing computer-aided design (CAD), marked by three major technological waves.
In 1982, John Walker and 15 co-founders launched Autodesk in Sausalito, California. They developed AutoCAD, the first mainstream CAD software capable of running on personal computers (PCs), breaking the monopoly of ultra-expensive industrial workstations.
In the 2000s, under the leadership of Carol Bartz, Autodesk transitioned from 2D drafting to interactive 3D modeling. The company acquired key technologies such as Revit (2002) for architecture and Alias/Wavefront (2006) with Maya for the film industry.
Since 2015, under the leadership of current CEO Andrew Anagnost, Autodesk has abandoned perpetual license sales to become a 100% cloud-based (SaaS) company, while massively integrating generative AI.
Its value proposition is built on the "Design & Make" concept: enabling the design of a project and then digitally manufacturing it end-to-end. This includes full interoperability, unifying the lifecycle of a project. For example, an architect designs a building in Revit, structural engineers analyze it in Robot, and construction teams manage it via the Autodesk Construction Cloud platform. Through AI and generative design, Autodesk helps its industrial clients, such as Airbus or Hyundai, create lighter parts that use fewer raw materials while being stronger. Additionally, Autodesk’s file formats, like .dwg for technical drawings, have become universal standards for communication between service providers on an international scale.
Its business model is based on the power of recurring SaaS revenue. Autodesk has successfully executed one of the most massive software transitions in the tech industry, moving from selling physical software boxes to a pure subscription model. Revenue comes from monthly, annual, or multi-year subscriptions, ensuring highly predictable cash flow (Annual Recurring Revenue). Autodesk no longer sells its software individually but instead offers thematic "Collections" (AEC, Manufacturing, M&E) that bundle all the software for a specific sector, increasing the average revenue per customer. For occasional users, Autodesk offers Flex Tokens, virtual tokens that allow access to specific software for a limited time (e.g., 24 hours of access to Maya). Finally, its cloud ecosystem and Marketplace allow it to host customer data on its servers (BIM 360, Forma) and take commissions on third-party applications developed by independent developers.

description:

Uniphore est une entreprise américaine de logiciels spécialisée dans l'intelligence artificielle (IA) d'entreprise, l'IA conversationnelle et l'automatisation. Fondée en 2008 par Umesh Sachdev et Ravi Saraogi, elle a son siège social à Palo Alto, en Californie, et possède une forte présence internationale dans plus de 20 pays, notamment aux États-Unis, en Inde, en Europe et au Moyen-Orient. L'offre centrale de la marque repose sur le Uniphore Business AI Cloud. Cette suite logicielle permet aux entreprises de connecter leurs données, d'affiner des modèles d'IA et de déployer des agents d'IA à grande échelle. Elle s'articule autour de trois piliers fondamentaux :Souveraineté : Elle propose une architecture unique « zéro copie » (zero-copy). L'IA convertit les bases de données en vecteurs ou en graphes sans jamais dupliquer ou déplacer les données originales hors de leur emplacement initial.Composabilité : La plateforme s'intègre de manière flexible avec n'importe quel modèle de langage (LLM ou SLM) ou source de données utilisateur.Sécurité : Un système robuste de garde-fous (guardrails) analyse chaque requête en temps réel pour empêcher les violations de données et encadrer le comportement de l'IA.Domaines d'applicationLa technologie d'Uniphore traite les interactions textuelles, visuelles et vocales (IA multimodale) pour optimiser les performances des entreprises :Expérience client (CX) : Analyse en temps réel des sentiments, du ton de la voix et des émotions des clients pour guider les agents humains ou déployer des agents virtuels autonomes.Opérations financières : Automatisation des processus de réconciliation, traitement des bons de commande et détection des pertes de revenus.Gestion des risques et conformité : Surveillance continue assistée par IA avec gouvernance intégrée à toutes les étapes de traitement des données.L'approche des Small Language Models (SLM)Face aux coûts prohibitifs des modèles d'IA géants d'infrastructure (Frontier Models), Uniphore prône une stratégie axée sur les petits modèles de langage personnalisés (SLM). L'entreprise utilise des techniques de réglage fin (fine-tuning) à faible rang pour adapter efficacement des modèles légers aux connaissances spécifiques d'une entreprise, réduisant ainsi drastiquement les coûts de calcul et de serveurs matériels tout en améliorant la gouvernance.
